signs.text: BLUE PLAQUE: The Bank of England was founded in 1694 to lend money to William III's government for its war with France, on an idea from a Scot, William Paterson. It has been on Threadneedle Street since 1734, hence its nickname, the Old Lady of Threadneedle Street. Since 1997 the Bank, not the government, has set the interest rate.
signs.title: The Bank of England

signs.text: BLUE PLAQUE: The South Sea Company was set up in 1711. In the summer of 1720 its shares soared past a thousand pounds, because people bought whatever was rising, and by the end of the year they had fallen to a fraction of that. Isaac Newton is said to have lost a fortune. A mania like it has been called a bubble ever since.
signs.title: The South Sea Bubble
Empire Windrush
signs.text: On 22 June 1948 the passengers of the Empire Windrush came ashore at Tilbury, down the Thames from here. Hundreds had sailed from the Caribbean, answering Britain's call for workers after the war. Many stayed first in a deep air-raid shelter at Clapham South, and the nearest labour exchange was in Brixton. Since 2018, 22 June has been Windrush Day.

signs.title: Claudia Jones
signs.text: Claudia Jones, born in Trinidad in 1915, founded the West Indian Gazette in Brixton in 1958 and organised a Caribbean carnival at St Pancras Town Hall in January 1959, one of the roots of the Notting Hill Carnival. She is buried in Highgate Cemetery, beside Karl Marx. Not a bad neighbour for an argument.

signs.title: Dadabhai Naoroji
signs.text: In 1892 Dadabhai Naoroji, a Parsi scholar and businessman from Bombay, was elected Liberal MP for Finsbury Central by just five votes, the first Asian member of the House of Commons. He argued that British rule was draining India's wealth, and India remembers him as its Grand Old Man.

signs.title: Noor Inayat Khan
signs.text: Noor Inayat Khan, daughter of an Indian Sufi teacher, grew up in Paris and wrote stories for children. In 1943 she was flown into occupied France as a secret wireless operator for the SOE, the first woman sent in that role. Betrayed and captured, she was killed at Dachau in 1944. She was awarded the George Cross, and her statue stands in Gordon Square.

signs.title: Mary Seacole
signs.text: Mary Seacole, born in Kingston, Jamaica, in 1805, learnt healing from her mother. When the War Office turned down her offer to nurse in the Crimean War, she went anyway, at her own expense, and ran the British Hotel near Balaclava, feeding and nursing soldiers. Her statue has stood outside St Thomas' Hospital since 2016.

signs.title: 59 Brick Lane
signs.text: The building on the corner of Brick Lane and Fournier Street went up in 1743 as a chapel for Huguenot refugees. It became a Methodist chapel, then in 1898 a synagogue for Jewish refugees from eastern Europe, and since 1976 it has been the Brick Lane Jamme Masjid, a mosque for the Bangladeshi community. Same walls, three faiths, one long story of arriving.

signs.title: Bevis Marks
signs.text: Jews were expelled from England in 1290 and allowed back under Oliver Cromwell in 1656. Bevis Marks Synagogue in the City opened in 1701, built by Sephardi Jews whose families had come from Spain and Portugal by way of Amsterdam. It is the oldest synagogue in Britain still in use.

signs.title: Southall
signs.text: Punjabi families began settling in Southall, in west London, in the 1950s, working in local factories and later at Heathrow. The station sign is written in English and in Punjabi's Gurmukhi script, and the Sri Guru Singh Sabha gurdwara, opened in 2003, is one of the largest Sikh temples outside India.
TOWER BRIDGE. Not London Bridge! That one is plainer. This one has two towers and a road that lifts for tall ships. In 1952 a double-decker bus jumped the gap while it was opening. The bus was fine.

THE THAMES. Britain's most famous river, with over 30 bridges in London alone. Once so smelly that Parliament hung soaked curtains at the windows, now clean enough for seals and the occasional confused porpoise.
PALACE OF WESTMINSTER. Where the nation argues about the nation. The clock tower is the Elizabeth Tower; the bell inside is Big Ben, named after either Sir Benjamin Hall or a boxer called Ben Caunt.
BIG BEN CLOCK. The clock keeps time by a pile of old pennies on the pendulum. To speed it up, add a penny. London has its priorities.

THE UNDERGROUND. The oldest metro in the world, opened 1863. The map is a diagram, not a map, because Harry Beck knew nobody cares where anything really is. They care about where to change. The mice are unionised.
THE VANE TOWER. Lord Vane's glass headquarters: 'a monument to a more orderly countryside'. The revolving door has never once let anyone in. It does, in fairness, rotate with great enthusiasm.

THE TOWER OF LONDON. A palace, a fortress, a prison and a treasury, with the Crown Jewels and a lot of stairs. The Yeoman Warders, or Beefeaters, live inside, give excellent tours, and will tell you off for petting a raven.

THE RAVENS. If the ravens leave the Tower, it is said, the kingdom will fall. So there are always at least six, their wings are gently trimmed, and they are very well fed. They are also rather smug about all of it.

SHAKESPEARE'S GLOBE. A faithful rebuild of the 1599 theatre, with a thatched roof and a yard where the 'groundlings' stand. The original burned down in 1613, after a stage cannon went off a bit enthusiastically.

THE SHARD. The tallest building in Western Europe when it opened in 2012: 310 metres of glass, shaped like a shard of glass, which is nicely honest. Please do not throw anything at it. You will be on camera.
THE LONDON EYE. A big wheel by the Thames. A ride takes 30 minutes and rises 135 metres. You can see Windsor Castle on a clear day, and your own breath on a cold one.
BOROUGH MARKET. A market has stood near here for a thousand years. You can buy cheese, bread, oysters, and a sausage roll bigger than your head. London food has come a very long way since the pie.
Road to Greenwich closed for resurfacing. Again. Sorry for any inconvenience.
BLUE PLAQUE: Charles Dickens, novelist, lived at 48 Doughty Street from 1837 to 1839 and wrote Oliver Twist there.
signs.title: Charles Dickens
The Great Fire
signs.text: The Great Fire of London began in Thomas Farriner's bakery on Pudding Lane on 2 September 1666 and burned for four days, destroying old St Paul's and most of the City. The Monument stands 202 feet tall, and 202 feet from where the bakery stood.

signs.title: Bazalgette's Sewers
signs.text: After the Great Stink of 1858, the engineer Joseph Bazalgette gave London a new sewer system, much of it hidden inside the Victoria Embankment. He made the pipes bigger than anyone thought necessary, just in case. London kept growing, and he was right.

signs.title: Bow Bells
signs.text: A true Cockney is said to be born within the sound of Bow Bells, the bells of St Mary-le-Bow in the City. Rhyming slang swaps a word for a rhyme, then drops the rhyme: apples and pears are stairs, and use your loaf means use your head, loaf of bread.

signs.title: Frost Fairs
signs.text: In the bitterest winters the Thames froze hard enough for Frost Fairs, with stalls, games and printing presses out on the ice. At the last one, in 1814, an elephant was led across the river below Blackfriars Bridge. The river has not frozen like that since.
NORTH: CAMBRIDGE, THE FENS, NORWICH AND THE BROADS. Up the old road to East Anglia: colleges, cathedrals, big skies and a great deal of mustard.
SOUTH: THE SOUTH DOWNS AND BRIGHTON. The London to Brighton road, 54 miles, mostly downhill once you're over the Downs.
EAST: THE KENT DOWNS, CANTERBURY AND DOVER. The old road to the Channel, walked by pilgrims, Romans and lorries.

signs.title: The City
signs.text: London's first stockbrokers did their deals in coffee houses, Jonathan's in Exchange Alley above all, after being thrown out of the Royal Exchange for bad manners. A proper Stock Exchange opened in 1801. The Square Mile still runs on coffee.

signs.title: The Royal Institution
signs.text: BLUE PLAQUE: Michael Faraday, a blacksmith's son who left school to be a bookbinder's apprentice, worked at the Royal Institution on Albemarle Street for over forty years. In 1831 he showed that moving a magnet through a coil of wire makes electricity flow: the idea inside every generator since. He began the Royal Institution's Christmas Lectures for young people in 1825, and they still run.

signs.title: Ada Lovelace
signs.text: BLUE PLAQUE: Ada Lovelace, mathematician and daughter of Lord Byron, lived in London. In 1843 she published notes on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine, a mechanical computer he designed but never finished. Her notes set out, step by step, how it could calculate a sequence called the Bernoulli numbers, and guessed that such a machine might one day compose music. In 1991 the Science Museum built Babbage's Difference Engine No. 2 from his drawings. It works.

signs.title: The Telegraph Catches a Killer
signs.text: In 1837 William Cooke and Charles Wheatstone patented an electric telegraph, and its wires were soon running beside the Great Western Railway out of Paddington. On 1 January 1845 John Tawell poisoned Sarah Hart at Salt Hill near Slough and caught the train to London. The telegraph got there first: a policeman was waiting at Paddington to follow him, and he was caught and hanged. News could now outrun a train.

signs.title: The World Wide Web
signs.text: Tim Berners-Lee, born in London in 1955, wrote a proposal in March 1989 at CERN, the physics laboratory near Geneva, for a web of linked pages anyone could read. In 1993 CERN put the web's software in the public domain, free for anyone to use. At the opening of the London 2012 Olympics he sat at a computer in the stadium and typed: This is for everyone.

signs.title: The First Mobile Call
signs.text: On New Year's Day 1985 the comedian Ernie Wise rang Vodafone's office in Newbury from St Katharine Docks, just beside the Tower, in the first public mobile phone call in Britain. Forty years on, nearly every adult in these isles carries one.

signs.title: DeepMind
signs.text: DeepMind was founded in London in 2010 by Demis Hassabis, Shane Legg and Mustafa Suleyman, and was bought by Google in 2014. Its offices are here at King's Cross. In March 2016 its program AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol, one of the best players of the board game Go, by four games to one. Nobody gave it the winning moves: it learnt from human games, then from millions of games against itself.
